en: *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*,
composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
There are three kinds of karma, namely: bodily karma, vocal karma, and mental karma;
this is from the Sūtra. Some say:

"The action performed by the body is called bodily karma, and the action consisting of verbal speech is called vocal karma; both of these possess both manifest (vijñapti) and non-manifest (avijñapti) aspects."
Karma associated with the mind is called mental karma; this karma is volition (*cetanā*).
Now, what dharma is that which the mind deliberates upon?
Since both body and mind possess form, what is the form of that which arises conditioned by the body?
This is the characteristic of bodily form.
If it is the characteristic of bodily form, why is it designated as "action performed by the body"?
Because the body, as a whole, is subsumed under the category of the body.

That which arises conditioned by the great elements of the body is called "bodily action"; here, a term used for a specific instance is applied to the general category, just as one might say "he dwells in the city" or "he dwells in the forest."
That arises through objective conditions.
Why? Because it is said that it excludes the movement of the lips and so forth, as well as their physical forms.
That mind does not arise conditioned by the movement of the lips and so forth, nor does it arise conditioned by form; rather, it arises conditioned by speech.
It does not take up a prior vow as its object;
that mind does not arise conditioned by a prior vow, but arises because of the causal conditions of a different retribution.
Why? Because the mind gives rise to action through speech and thought, which others perceive.
What are their characteristics?
What is meant by "long and so forth"?
What are "long and so forth"?
It refers to the perception of long and so forth.
To which sense-base (āyatana) does this belong?
It is subsumed under the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana).
Are length and so forth the color of atoms (paramāṇu)?
Is it like a collection of atoms?
Or is it a single entity that pervades color and the other [sensory objects]?
If length and so forth were the color of atoms, then those lengths and so forth could be apprehended part by part, just as color is apprehended part by part.
If they were like atoms gathered together, what difference would there be between those material atoms and their collection?
There would be no difference at all between those atoms and the collection.
If a single entity were to pervade [the qualities of] color and so forth, then that single entity would also pervade length and so forth.
If a single entity were to pervade each and every part, it should be perceivable in all of them, because it would be present in every location.

If they were not one, they would have to be grasped part by part; thus, the *āgama* teaching that ten atoms aggregate to form a subtle particle (*paramāṇu*) would be undermined, and the Buddhist Dharma would be destroyed.
Furthermore, according to the distinct doctrine of Kaṇāda, it would result in the grasping and aggregation of atoms.

When one sees from one side, there arises the cognition of length; when seeing narrowly, there arises the cognition of shortness. When seeing correctly, there arises the cognition of squareness; when seeing all around, there arises the cognition of roundness. When seeing from the center, there arises the cognition of height; when seeing from below, there arises the cognition of lowness; when seeing from level, there arises the cognition of correctness. When seeing from various angles, there arises the cognition of irregularity.
When one sees various carpets and brocades, they are seen as they truly are, and thus cognitions arise corresponding to their respective forms and characteristics.
Those diverse objects cannot be perceived as a single unity, just as there is a differentiation in colors.
If, furthermore, you should think that all locations and all forms [are substantial entities], this is not the case;
for such forms do not consist of any distinct substance. Color is also like this:
when one perceives length, shortness, and so forth as abiding in a location, it is established—without fault—just as in the cases of a tree, a bird, or an ant.
If this were so, why is it that one does not see forms when they are obscured or distant, yet sees their gathered shapes and characteristics?
And why is it that one sees all previously unseen shapes and characteristics, such as trees, rows, and so forth?
One sees that collection of activities but does not see its specific form; therein there is no distinct entity.
Within that assembly, whether due to darkness or distance, one does not perceive two kinds [of objects]. Although one sees, one does not clearly discern what it is; what, then, is it that one sees?
Although one sees those forms, they are not clearly discerned; thus one should know that this definition of "mind" (*manas*) as a mental image is not established.
Furthermore, some say: the mind arises taking those [objects] as its condition, and because it moves toward them, it is called "mind."
What is the meaning of "arising by depending upon that"? It means the exclusion of the movement of the lips and so forth.
For what reason is it called "going"?
That which is directed toward that direction—
by which sense-base (*āyatana*) is it subsumed?
It is subsumed by the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
How is it known that this [element] goes from here to that place?
It is by seeing no difference.

Just as fire, snow, bitter wine, the sun, and so forth, having entered as causes and conditions for transformation and ripening, emerge immediately; though no change is yet seen, it is not the case that there is no difference.
Just as when fuel is being burned, one does not perceive any difference in the flames among grasses, woods, and so forth, yet it is not that the flames are not different.
If there were no change at the initial moment, there would likewise be no change later, because those causes and conditions would not be distinct.
If the fuel, grass, and so forth are uneven in their coarseness or fineness, the dimensions of the flames, as well as their brightness and heat, will all differ and not be uniform.
Since they are seen to be dissimilar, the principle that [the fire] moves toward that direction is inconsistent with reason.
If there were no cause for cessation, why would the mind and mental factors not persist?
What causes and conditions lead to the cessation of sound, lamps, and so forth?
The same applies to all other things.
If that [phenomenon] perishes through its own causes and conditions, why do the causes and conditions of other phenomena not likewise perish?
Furthermore, just as that phenomenon lacks causes and conditions, so it is with all others.
If, when first entering a fire, the colors of grass, wood, and so forth remain as they were without change, and later they are likewise, there should be no difference.
Why is it that the light of a lamp or the sound of a bell, upon being first touched by wind or hand, are immediately extinguished or ceased?

It is not that this can extinguish it, nor that this can cease it; if it were like fire burning wood, or color being extinguished, why would there be no difference between the initial entry and the subsequent exit?
Since external conditions do not differ [in their nature], the objects undergoing transformation should not possess the distinctions of slight, moderate, or intense degrees of ripening.
Furthermore, by what cause could an object in its initial stage of transformation undergo such change?
It is illogical for a single condition to be both the cause of arising and the cause of cessation.

Two phenomena cannot be established by a single cause; likewise, there must be a further cause for cessation in the interim, such that, as previously explained, through the process of grasping and abandoning, they evolve within a different continuum.
This should be understood thus: if cessation has a cause, then non-existence (the state of cessation) does not lack a cause, just as the arising of the mind and other phenomena [requires causes].
The phenomenon of cessation is not established, because all phenomena possess causes, whereas cessation itself would be causeless.

For example, in the case of fire, snow, bitter wine, the sun, and so forth, which act as the causal conditions for transformation and ripening—if cessation were to have a cause, then cessation would be like form; thus, there would be no such thing as a non-existent phenomenon that undergoes cessation through causal conditions.

Arising is likewise without cause; yet one perceives that distinct phenomena are the actual causes for the arising of this phenomenon. Just as the mind in the preceding moment relates to the mind in the succeeding moment through intermediate transformation, or as milk becomes curd, grape juice becomes wine, and wine becomes vinegar—thus, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that possesses a mark of abiding.
The object that abides has no movement; where there is no movement, there is abiding.
If one views it in this way, what is that which is seen?
It is the object located at this very place.
Is it not because one sees that place as newly appearing?
That place appears as new when seen, just like a shadow upon grass; it is not that a shadow from that place is seen here.
Just as the sun abides, so does the sun revolve at varying distances, and its shadow is seen revolving with corresponding increase and decrease.
When the sun is at a certain location, it is obscured by shadows and thus cannot be seen.
Suppose, however, someone were to raise this objection:
"What kind of object is this?"
If that previous object were to turn toward this direction, one would answer that person:
"What kind of object is this that you speak of in terms of 'moving'? An object that abides in such a manner cannot have motion."

If objects do not undergo transformation, then they would remain as they are, destroyed only by external conditions; subsequently, one would perceive them as different through moment-to-moment cognitions of difference.
If there were no cognition of difference, those objects would not be distinct;
since the cognition is not the object itself, why not say that the objects are different?
Since these two kinds [of movement] are both invisible, the meaning of "going" as a functional process is not established.
In reality, there is no such thing as going.

The nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is that they perish of their own accord moment by moment; rather, it is when a causal factor arises within the interim and the mind acts as the cause, that the movement of the hands, feet, and so forth is designated as "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*). As for "verbal" and "mental" [action], they are likewise established.
The disciple Rishya says: "To which base (āyatana) does this belong?
It is included within the base of form (rūpāyatana)."
For what reason?

Just as that which is not seen by the eye, such as the color blue, cannot be spoken of as "intention" if another person sees it, how can it be spoken of as "intention" when another person does not see it?
How is its existence known?
How does the wind element of the mind arise, moving and circulating through different locations within the body?
This wind element moves because it arises due to causes and conditions from various directions.
Why is this? Just as blades of grass and leaves incline according to the wind element, so too is the movement [of consciousness].
Since it arises in different locations and the power of movement is not established, what is the use of making such distinctions?
Regarding the cause for the subsequent arising of such a body: the mind gives rise to the wind-element; this is what is called "mind" (*manas*).
How can that which is not the mind be called "mind"?

According to the Dharma of the Śākyaputrīyas, the sphere of mental contact (*dharmāyatana*) is neither wholesome nor unwholesome. When that mind arises in a different location within the body, this arising is called "mind."
If it were as you say, then the mind would consist only of appearances and lack substantial reality, while the body would be predominant.
Furthermore, the mind would not be the mind, being like tastes and other such objects for others.

The Dharma of the Śākyaputrīyas is not thus; since tastes and so forth are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and because they give rise to matter within the mind, that [mind] can be called "intention" (manas).
It is not born from that mind, but is born from its own wind-element.
The Dharma of the Śākyaputrīyas is not like this: the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
That form arises in that place; the mind cannot be apprehended there.
If those things exist, the gods may obtain them through offerings; if those things do not exist, the gods cannot bestow them, and thus they cannot be obtained.
Since living beings are no different [from one another], who could bring about such a difference?
Those [objects] such as form cannot be apprehended in the same way that the eye sees; their arising is not like that.
Since they cannot be seen, how can one speak of "mind"?
This has already been explained: just as their arising is not like that, so too has form already been explained.
Only non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is the karma of this body.
What is called "non-informative"?
It refers to the forms included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), such as fear and so forth.
How can that which is "unmanifest" (avijñapti) be said to be unmanifest?
If it were to arise in conjunction with the mind in the desire realm, then one would know it to belong to the form realm, and thus it would be distinct from the mind.
Furthermore, at times when there is no mind, both fear and non-fear would be lost along with the mind; yet, once received, its force is never lost thereafter.
The *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* states:
"A bhikṣu remains silent; how, then, can he be guilty of lying?
Furthermore, neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma could not be established [under such conditions].
Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is of two kinds, namely wholesome and unwholesome.

At that moment, non-informative action arises in conjunction [with informative action]; just as those [informative] bodily and vocal actions are analyzed as being material form (*rūpa*), if they are either wholesome or unwholesome, both [the wholesome and unwholesome aspects] are not established [as independent entities].
Why is this? Because once the body is discarded, it is severed; thus, in future lives, pleasant and unpleasant fruits cannot be obtained.
Furthermore, some say:
If past karma exists, why is it not established?
If past karma were to obtain two kinds of retributions—pleasant and unpleasant—in a future life, this would be like a carbuncle growing upon an existing abscess.
Regarding past karma that exists in the past, this is called "existence before and non-existence after.
As the Tathāgata has said:
"Though a hundred eons may pass, karma is never lost."
"When causes and conditions meet in harmony, at that time the retribution ripens.
What does this verse mean?
That which can grant retribution is the meaning of "non-loss" (avipraṇāśa).
Having thus explained the first half-verse, who would not believe that the fruit is attained after a long duration?
What is the meaning of "attaining the fruit"?
It should be understood as follows: it is like a grain of rice seed that evolves through a continuous succession, or it abides in its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If that which abides in its own characteristic were able to produce a fruit, it would not perish and should therefore constantly produce that fruit.
Since it lacks its own characteristic, it is called "perished.
Furthermore, it is not the case that once something has been produced, it does not act again.
How is it that they do not act?
The fruit is not bestowed twice.
Why is it not bestowed?
Because it has already been given;
that which has already been given cannot be given again, just as once a thing has arisen, it does not arise again.
Why, then, would its similar fruit (*sabhāga-phala*) not likewise be given again?
How is it that once the retribution has been fully bestowed, the causal conditions for the arising of phenomena lack such power?

For one who has exhausted the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), the subsequent thought-moment that exhausts the outflows does not bestow retribution; how then can it be said that [the outflows] are extinguished at a later time?
It is not by such power that the fruit-retribution is produced. If the causal seed possesses power with respect to the fruit, one may say that the power of the cause can bestow the fruit-retribution.
If certain persons possess the past, they must also possess the future; for what reason, then, does the future not bestow fruit-retribution?
"What things exist at all times?
At what time are they non-existent? He spoke thus:
If the fruit were to ripen upon attaining the conditions for its assembly, this would not be so.
By what power of person, at what time, and by what power of thing would this person’s fruit ultimately fail to be accomplished?
The notion that there exists past karma which attains its retribution in a future life is thus untenable.
Furthermore, some say:

"Those wholesome and unwholesome karmas of body, speech, and so forth, within the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-santāna*), are perfumed by mental factors; whether they are termed 'accumulation' (*upacaya*) or 'non-perishing' (*avipraṇāśa*), one subsequently obtains desirable or undesirable fruits in a future life."
If mental karma were to arise and perish independently of the mind, or if it did not permeate the mind, how could its retribution be obtained in future lives?
It is like when a person recites [a text] and remembers it for a long time.
Regarding those objects such as visual forms and so forth, for one who practices in this way,
by what dharma are they perfumed?
What is it that is recollected?
When one observes such things as recitation, from where does the mind arise in the subsequent moment of recollection?
Furthermore, when the samādhi of cessation has occurred and the initial mind has already perished, from where does the mind arise in the subsequent moment?
If one coats the flowers of that *laṅgaka* tree with the juice of purple minerals, both [the flower and the fruit] will perish together.
Thus, in the interim, what substance could have stained the fruit so that a red core subsequently arises?

It should be understood that hearing and reflecting upon the Dharma is likewise so: through the power of the mental continuum and the power of perfuming, there is a transformation that results in the attainment of fruit in future lives.
This is like the juice of purple mineral dye staining the flowers of the *maṇḍūka* tree, resulting in red fibers within the fruit.
Because bodily karma thus continues to permeate the mind, that mind cannot be said to be directly confronted by [the nature of] the wholesome or unwholesome.
If this person performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds, the resulting pleasant or unpleasant fruits will correspond to the power of those actions; they do not correspond to anything else.

Furthermore, if karma ceases yet its fruit is obtained in a future life because of the continuity of the mind, how could it be that when there is no mind—such as in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or the mindless state (*asaṃjñi*)—the continuity of the mind is severed, and yet the retribution of prior karma arises upon that very body at a later time?
Furthermore, some say:
"That [perfuming] is obtained through the perfuming of the mental continuum (*citta-saṃtāna*).
[If so,] where does that cessation-samādhi continue?
Regarding the causal conditions for the initial moment of samāpatti:
how is it that [the mind] has long since ceased?
What are its causal conditions?
I have already previously explained that the fruit is obtained in the past; where, then, could such a mind arise in the interim?
Furthermore, some say:
"The seeds of the material faculties (rūpīndriya) are obtained upon those very seeds."
The mind and its mental factors depend upon two bases: namely, within the body of mind and within the body of the material sense-faculties.
Thus, in this sequence, as the mind takes dharmas as its object, mental consciousness arises.
If there were no mind during the interval, how could it arise?

Furthermore, one should understand that the seeds obtain the designation of "mental characteristics"; thus, the cause is spoken of as the effect, just as in the case of the contact of hunger and thirst.
How is it that both the mind and its mental factors each possess two kinds of seeds?
Within a single kind of seed, there cannot be two kinds of sprouts.
Just as one does not see multiple productions arising from a single cause, the same fault applies here as well.
In the mindless samādhi, the mind of perception is severed; how then can the fruit of karma be obtained at a later time?
This is one flaw in this casket.
What kind of casket is this?
Regarding the mindless samādhi (acittaka-samādhi) of any person whatsoever,
others further say it is the mindful samādhi (sacittaka-samādhi). For instance, within the assembly of five hundred arhats of the Vibhāṣā, the venerable Vāsūmitra stated:
If certain individuals claim that the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is mindless, they incur this fault; for my cessation samādhi is possessed of mind.
To provide scriptural proof, he cites a sūtra which says:
"While bodily formations cease and the sense faculties do not function, consciousness does not depart from the body."
Furthermore, what consciousness does that person believe in and accept?
Some say it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The Tathāgata has taught that mental consciousness arises through the conditions of the mind; the coming together of these three is called contact (*sparśa*), and contact arises simultaneously with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
How can there be mental consciousness without the conjunction of the three factors?
Or how can there be their conjunction without contact (*sparśa*)?
Or again, how can there be contact without feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)?
If one intends for the cessation of feeling to be called "extinction," why does the Tathāgata state in the sūtras that "feeling is always conditioned by craving"?
It is not the case that all feelings have craving as their cause; the same should apply to contact (*sparśa*).
Not all contacts (sparśa) have feeling (vedanā) as their cause and condition; the Tathāgata has also explained this meaning specifically in the sūtras.

Ignorance gives rise to contact, contact gives rise to feeling, and feeling serves as the cause and condition for craving (tṛṣṇā). Nowhere is it said that contact is separate from feeling and perception (saṃjñā).
If one does not speak in this way, those faults will ensue and cannot be avoided; for it must be said that when the three factors are complete, there is "conjunction.
Without those three factors, perception and feeling do not arise.
If it were not so, there would be no such contact even within samādhi; where, then, could feeling and perception exist?
Furthermore, some say that there is only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
What is that consciousness?
Is it wholesome, defiled, afflicted, or neutral?
This point shall now be explained.
If it were wholesome, it would be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment; yet how could there be no contact (*sparśa*) when there is wholesome non-attachment?

If the power of causes and conditions at that very moment were wholesome, it would not be dissociated from a wholesome mind and so forth; thus, for the three types of minds to give rise to the power of wholesome states and so on, the turning of the mind would be without cause.
If it were that which is defiled, how could it not be associated with afflictions?
If it were the defiling affliction, how could there be no contact?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata spoke in the *Daśa-praśna-sūtra*:
If there are the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, all such aggregates have contact as their causal condition.
Even the concentration of non-perception is free from defilement, how much more so the concentration of cessation.
If that [state] is undefiled-neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta), what kind of thing is it?
Is it born of maturation (vipākaja), or is it deportment (airyāpathika), or is it craftsmanship (śailpasthānika), or is it transformation (nairmāṇika)?
Now we should question him:

if this were born of retribution, how could the mind of the samādhi of the Peak of Existence descend as far as the eighth stage, with the retributive consciousness of the desire realm suspended in between, yet still maintaining a continuity of mind?
Furthermore, there arises an immovable mind; how does it continue?
As asked of the Tathāgata in the Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra:
"In the samādhi of arising and ceasing, by how many contacts is one touched?"
The Tathāgata replied:
"Venerable Kauṣṭhila!
There are three contacts by which one is touched: namely, the immovable, the signless, and the non-existent."
Previously, one made a formal resolve to enter the *nirodha-samādhi* with force, and the preceding mind made a formal resolve not to arise until the appointed time has passed.
What is the meaning of this?
How do they all take [the object] as their condition?

At the conclusion of the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the karma of the desire realm previously perfumed the mind and receives its retribution.
Why does the preceding mind not receive this retribution? For what reason?
If the matter of the prior retribution were severed there and did not continue, how could the subsequent mind continue?
Furthermore, if there is no contact with the physical bases of deportment and so forth in that place, how can the mind take those deportments as its object?
Those conditioned wholesome states—the nine successive attainments and the eight liberations—are not associated with it; those undefiled minds and indeterminate minds do not continue from it.

One enters the cessation of perception and feeling by relying on the samādhi of the Peak of Existence, taking the meditative absorption of cessation as the object of recollection. If there were mental consciousness when one has entered the absorption of cessation, what would it take as its object?
If it takes cessation as its object, how can it not be wholesome?
If it is wholesome, then it must be associated with non-attachment.
If it is so associated, why would it not obtain the causal conditions for contact?

If one enters the samādhi of cessation with a different object of focus, how could it be that in the interim there is a corresponding distracted mind, which one’s own mind discriminates as being indeterminate?
These two types [of states] are mutually incompatible; thus, one does not understand the true meaning of the Āgamas.
That master of the treatise exultantly declared:
"Even within the samādhi of cessation, there is still mental consciousness that performs such discrimination.
How, then, can that be a 'mindful' (sacittaka) samādhi?"
As the Sūtra masters explain with faith, how do the Sūtra masters explain it with faith?

They say that the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), in which all seeds are secretly bound by karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), continues without interruption; the retributive consciousness, characterized by the mark of destruction, proceeds in succession from one place of birth to another, continuing even until nirvāṇa without being severed.
If it were as you say, one could claim that there exists a mind distinct from the six groups of consciousness; therefore, [the mind] would not cease to function.

However, at the very moment of first entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the power of the predominant mind causes all seeds to become concealed and suppressed; for this reason, it is called "mindless."
There are two kinds of mind:
first, the mind that accumulates all seeds; second, the mind that is destroyed by various objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Because it is free from the second kind of mind, it is called "mindless" (*acitta*), just as a bed with only one leg is called a "legless bed" because it lacks the remaining legs.

When those seeds are closed, the evolving consciousness of retribution manifests in weak, medium, or superior degrees—like water, heat, or the momentum of a released arrow—which carries [the influence] from this point to that. When the period for those seed-consciousnesses arrives, they arise again; according to various causes and conditions, they become distinct at a later time.
Regarding the various seeds, the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is the storehouse (*ālaya*).

Those respective distinct cognitions (*vijñapti*) arise simultaneously with their corresponding dharmas, mutually perfuming one another as wholesome or unwholesome; thus, according to that sequence, the power of the seeds is perfumed and continues to evolve in succession.
Just as it is perfumed by those powers, one obtains various pleasant and unpleasant fruits in future bodies.
Because this consciousness is the causal condition, it is thus said:
"The seeds of this mind-consciousness / Flow in an infinite succession."
From the causes and conditions within one's own mind, various seeds arise through their respective powers.
These proceed in succession without being lost; when the time arrives, they yield their fruit, just as the *maṇḍūka* flower appears when its stamens are smeared with pigment.
Regarding this meaning, the Tathāgata spoke in verse within that *Gambhīra-rahasya-vimokṣa-mahāyāna-sūtra*:
“The ālayavijñāna seed, Deep, subtle, and dense in its activity,
Is not taught to the foolish, For fear they would falsely conceptualize it as a self.”
What does this verse clarify?
Because there is further a subtle and dense grasping of the body within that state, it is called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness);
because it is the locus of reliance for the seeds of all phenomena, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
It is called the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) because it is the karmic fruition of past lives.
If that consciousness did not exist, by what would the body be perceived?
As long as the body has not yet perished, this consciousness pervades the entire body without departing; there is no other consciousness besides it.
If there is nothing further to oppose it, what thing could serve as the antidote to the root of afflictions?
How could the root of afflictions be counteracted?
This is because there is no duality of phenomena.
Defiled conduct, wholesome conduct, and untainted mental conduct—through the continuity of such [conduct], birth in the formless realm occurs.
What is that conduct?
Upon what retribution does it depend?
If that were so, one should also be able to attain the practice of that which is without retribution, yet that is not the case.

For example, when an Anāgāmin who has cultivated and accumulated the exhaustion of outflows at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) brings forth the untainted state (anāsrava) of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), how could there be any "mine" (mamakāra) regarding the Peak of Existence from which he would not fall back?
The harmonious combination of the various factors is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); there is no other distinct entity.
That dharma is merely the continued functioning of a force similar to the retributive aggregates (*vipākaskandha*), and there is no separate substance.
The similar force is like that of a stalk of rice; one should understand that there is yet another consciousness, just as it is said that "consciousness exists.
What is its object?
Regarding the indeterminate conditions:

why is it said that the condition for consciousness is not determinate? Furthermore, how can there be a consciousness distinct from [ordinary] consciousness, such as the cessation samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?
As that Venerable One, the disciple of the Copper-Colored One, spoke of the *bhavāṅga-vijñāna*, others have further stated that this is the *mūla-vijñāna*.
Under which aggregate of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) is this meaning subsumed? It is subsumed under the aggregate of clinging that is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How, then, are the words, phrases, and syllables of this *sūtra* explained?
Which consciousnesses constitute the aggregate of grasping? They are the six groups of consciousness.
As it is said that "volitional formations condition consciousness," what kind of consciousness is this?
Because of the six bodies of consciousness.
One should remember this teaching on the dharmas, just as with that aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
What is the aggregate of formations?
Because it consists of the six volitions (*ṣaḍ-cetanā-kāya*), no other dharmas are included; furthermore, what would there be to remember?
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other sūtras all state that the Tathāgata [taught this].
I do not speak of a "self" to foolish ordinary people, for I fear they would conceptualize it.
For what reason do they thus conceptualize?
It is because those conditioned formations circulate everywhere, and I fear that people might not understand this.
If it is said in this way— that based upon various objects of perception, there is superior and excellent cognition—
and if that is associated with the antidotes to the afflictions, then the consciousness of seeds is described as being both defiled and pure.
If one were to explain such consciousness by way of its result while failing to explain the causal consciousness, that would be a distorted explanation.
Because of this principle, there is the consciousness of the body.

Furthermore, there is the consciousness of the body as explained in successive order; this meaning is consistent, for it is not because all sūtras must be interpreted as consistent with their stated meaning that they are so. Thus, it is not the case that all sūtras speak in this manner.
Do not conclude that the ālaya-vijñāna does not exist simply because it is not mentioned in all the sūtras.
Thus, two kinds of mental consciousness flow together in one place; these are what are called the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna) and the evolving consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna).
If this were so, what fault would there be?
If there were two distinct streams of consciousness continuing in succession, then there would necessarily be two sentient beings, just as there are multiple consciousnesses within a single body.

It is not possible for that seed and its fruit to function in mutual correspondence, because the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna) flows on as a stream; thus it can perfume a distinct consciousness, whereas such is not the case for the intermediate body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna).
If it were thus, there would be no fault.

Furthermore, there is the view that seeds and those produced from seeds are distinct and subject to destruction, such as the various roots from which *śaruka*, *utpala*, and other flowers arise; whether they are seen or not seen, it is not so.
If it is explained in this way, there is no fault; thus, the ālayavijñāna truly exists.
For what reason do the six consciousnesses not depend upon a self, and what constitutes "consciousness"?
If it were to evolve through the causal conditions of the continuity of the ālayavijñāna, how would it differ from that?
If it were a single entity and ultimately immobile, how could consciousness and the like undergo perfuming?
It is like the juice of purple lac dye perfuming the flowers of the *maṅgala* tree;

if there were no perfuming, there would be no further excellence of the dharma. How could one first know things such as the practice of desire, or how could one remember and know that desire and so forth have grown over a long period of time?
Since there is no self within me, from where would the mind arise later?
If there were no self, what power would the mind have to rely upon that self for its conceptualization?
If there were a self, how could that mind arise in succession?
If it arises through the power of various causes and conditions, how can this be known?
If its arising, abiding, and transformation occur by means of that power, what kind of phenomenon is it?
If this were the case—that dissimilar things co-dependently abide—then it would contradict the meaning of the Āgamas, which state that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*).

Thus, such irrational conceptualization and deliberation by one’s own mind, which calculates a self, perfumes the *ālayavijñāna* through thought in an uninterrupted succession; consequently, the principle of obtaining results in a future body is established, rather than [results arising] from the bodily and vocal actions as they are conventionally described.
Furthermore, these actions of body and speech do not contradict the Sūtras which speak of the three types of action.
How is this so? This meaning does not contradict what was taught by the Tathāgata; thus, there is no fault.
If one can speak in this manner, how is it that there is no fault?
This point shall now be explained.
For what reason are the three types of karma taught?
What is the body? What is karma? In what sense is it called "body"?
In what sense is it called "karma"? What is bodily karma?
The same applies to verbal karma as well.
For what reason are bodily actions and so forth mentioned, while eye-action is not?
For what reason is this point stated?

It is shown that the ten paths of wholesome action are subsumed within the three types of action; this is taught extensively because one fears people might study the threefold precepts like the son of Viriñci, thinking that these three types of action are performed by the body alone, and not by speech or mind, thus making a distinction only for one of them.

Furthermore, for the sake of others, he explains the characteristics of bodily action (*kāyakarman*): the body is a collection of the sense faculties (*indriya*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and that which is produced by the primary elements; therefore, it is called "bodily action. This refers to the meaning of the accumulation of volition (*cetanā*). It is termed the "body" as a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) produced by the primary elements.
Furthermore, some say:
"The body is called 'impure' because it is a composite of impure substances.
The bodies of those heavenly beings cannot be called 'bodies' [in that sense]."
Mental activity is called mental karma; the accumulation of activity through bodily movement is called bodily karma.
Volition (*cetanā*) is of three kinds: namely, deliberation, determination, and engagement.
If one moves with the body, the cause for the continuity of that body arises; that which is impelled by the wind element is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Excluding the intermediate phrase, [the paths of action]—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—are explained as being like *sāra* oil or like wind-blown dust.
How is it that volition (cetanā) is included within the category of that body?

Bodily action consists of movement—namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and because that bodily movement brings about the continuity of bodily form, it can be called "action" (*kṛta*). It is like a thief who sets fire to a village, burns the firewood and grass, and cooks the rice.
How can volition (*cetanā*) further be called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*)?
It is called a path of action because it proceeds along the path of evil karma; alternatively, it is called a path of action because it sets the body in motion.
The three types of volitional karma can be designated as "action," for when that volition persists and maintains its force, it results in killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is said that bodily action (kāyakarman) is either wholesome or unwholesome;
it is further explained that this is due to that volition (cetanā), which constitutes the meaning of the corresponding engagement in the cycle of worldly transmigration.
If one considers such wholesome and unwholesome karma, why does the Sūtra state:
"The three types of bodily action are volition (*cetanā*), karma, and accumulated action (*abhisamskāra*)"?
Unwholesome [actions] give rise to suffering because they result in the retribution of suffering; thus, they abide and are maintained through that gateway.
As for their objective referent (*ālambana*), this is the Buddha’s intention.
Because that volition (*cetanā*) is distinct, it is called mental action (*manas-karman*); it is associated solely with the mind and does not manifest as bodily or vocal [action].
For what reason does the Tathāgata speak of volitional action (*cetanā-karman*)?
As previously stated, there are three kinds of volition.
Of those two kinds of volition, the third is that which proceeds toward [an object].
That volition is karma, and speech is an echo.

If an echo can be understood, that karma is called "speech" because it is explained through the characteristics of names and phrases associated with the movement of volition; it is called "speech" because it is explained as having the sense of recollection.
Karma is as previously explained.
Because speech arises from karma, it is called verbal karma (*vākkarman*), excluding the intermediate words.
Consciousness and mind are termed "mind" (*manas*); the mind arises everywhere.
The objective sphere is also mind; the rest is as previously explained.

If within bodily action there must be volition (*cetanā*), then when it is different from the mind or when there is no mind, at that time there is no volition. How, then, could there be fear or fearlessness?
When the perfuming of thought is unimpaired, one attains fearlessness regarding fear; such deliberation is supreme.
If there were fear or fearlessness, the mind would give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Since that mind is what is being perfumed, how could it be destroyed?
Just as one knows for oneself what is negated and what is not negated, volition (*cetanā*) is further without a cause; what, then, could destroy it?
If one abandons fear and abandons the absence of fear, volition is its cause, and the mind gives rise to conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, there is another cause for relinquishment: the karma of eye, speech, and so forth.
It has already been stated that the karma of awareness is not the karma of volitional construction.
What, then, is the karma of awareness?
This refers to the activity of mental attention (*manasikāra*). What is it that performs this activity?
And by what power do the eye and the other faculties proceed in their successive order?
The Tathāgata spoke of the three karmas, Which are accomplished through the Dharma and its meaning;
I understand that karma brings about merit, And vow that all beings may attain Buddhahood. *Treatise on the Accomplishment of Karma* (Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa)
